{{italic title}}
'''''Die Rechenmaschinen''''', by Ernst Martin, and its English translation, '''''The Calculating Machines (Die Rechenmaschinen): Their History and Development''''', are books on [[Mechanical calculator|mechanical desktop calculators]] from prior to [[World War II]].

==Publication history==
''Die Rechenmaschinen'', the original book by Martin, was published in 1925, and revised in 1937. Both editions are very rare.{{r|booth}} Little is known about Martin beyond these books.{{r|tweedale}}

The 1925 edition was edited and translated into English by [[Peggy A. Kidwell]] and Michael R. Williams, and published in 1992 by the [[MIT Press]] as the final 16th volume of its The Charles Babbage Institute Reprint Series for the History of Computing ({{ISBN|0-262-13278-8}}). Kidwell and Williams chose this edition, rather than the revised edition, because of "the rarity of the books and the poor condition of the illustrations in extant copies".{{r|booth}} Indeed, they were only able to locate three copies of Martin's book.{{r|tweedale}}

The book and its translation includes many illustrations,{{r|swade}} and
the translation preserves some idiosyncrasies of the original work, including a set of advertisements for calculating machines at the end of the book.{{r|booth|swade}}

==Topics==
After an introduction grouping calculating machines into seven types,{{r|bsts}}
the book describes over 200 machines,{{r|swade}} comprising "almost every desk-top calculator available before World War II",{{r|booth}} ordered chronologically.{{r|bsts}} It also contains biographical information about some of the people who contributed to the design of these machines, including [[Blaise Pascal]], [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz]], and [[Giovanni Poleni]].{{r|booth}}

==Audience and reception==
At the time Martin wrote the book, "mechanical calculating machines were a symbol of high-tech sophistication in the workplace"; reviewer Jonathan Samuel Golan suggests that it was aimed at collectors rather than historians,{{r|golan}} while the editors of the ''[[Bulletin of Science, Technology & Society]]'' suggest that instead its purpose was to inform the public.{{r|bsts}} Nowadays, reviewer A. D. Booth suggests that readers of the book are likely to be people who once used these machines, looking back at them with nostalgia,{{r|booth}} while the ''Bulletin'' editors point to new use by collectors,{{r|bsts}} and Golan instead suggests that it can be used to study the history of a bygone technology.{{r|golan}}

In terms of its content, Booth complains that the contributions of [[Samuel Morland]] are overlooked, and that Morland's calculator was at least the equal of Pascal's in priority and quality.{{r|booth}} Similarly, [[Doron Swade]] notes the omission of the work of [[Wilhelm Schickard]], earlier than that of both Morland and Pascal, but excuses this lapse by noting that Schickard's work was forgotten and only rediscovered after Martin's book was published.{{r|swade}} Golan writes that the descriptions of older calculating machines are "cursory" and secondhand, while the later ones seem to be copied from advertisements.{{r|golan}}

Booth praises the quality of the translation, and calls the newly reprinted edition "an invaluable window on the past".{{r|booth}} Similarly, Golan calls it "a valuable document, providing a fascinating portrait of the state of the art".{{r|golan}} Swade is more cautious, pointing to the book's clear biases, but still noting its value as "reference material for collectors and curators as well as historians".{{r|swade}}
